prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The monocular depth map depicts a cramped bathroom layout where the camera wearer looks down at a small child (~0.3–0.5 m away, bottom center) standing directly in front of a sink counter (~0.5–0.8 m away) lined with bottles on the left and a storage caddy, toilet paper roll, and toilet (~0.8–1.3 m away) on the right, all within arm's reach of both the wearer and the child. In frames 1–3, the child's head and a toothbrush held near the child's right side (under 0.4 m away) appear bright in the foreground, while a shower curtain hangs at the upper left (~0.3–0.6 m) and a wall mirror sits behind the counter (~0.8–1.0 m away); in frames 4–5, the camera wearer turns and tilts rightward and upward so the child moves down and out of the lower-left frame while the sink, toilet tank, bowl, and adjacent right wall (~0.5–1.5 m) dominate the view. In frames 1–3, the child faces and looks upward toward the camera wearer while occluding the central sink basin, whereas in the mirror reflection the child's back and the wearer's torso (standing right behind the child, <0.3 m apart) are partially visible. Compared to the heavily yellow-tinted and blurred RGB strip, the depth map much more clearly separates the 3D silhouettes of the upright toothbrush in frames 2–3, the cluster of counter bottles, and the stepped geometry of the sink counter versus the lower toilet bowl in frame 5. However, the depth map is unreliable on the mirror in frames 4–5—where it hallucinates a deep black void (>2 m) for the reflected room instead of the flat mirror plane (~0.9 m)—and in frame 1 where the blurred child's head merges smoothly into the sink background.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map isolates the foreground child (`person`, ~0.3–0.5 m away in bottom center) in frames 1–3 and several toiletries (`bottle`, ~0.5–0.7 m away at middle-left) resting on the sink counter ~0.2–0.3 m to the child's right (viewer's left), all within arm's reach of the camera wearer and child. In frame 1, it also segments the mirror reflection at the top left (~1.2–1.6 m optical distance, ~0.8 m physical distance to the glass), showing the camera wearer's torso and child's head (`person`) facing the mirror (with the reflection facing back toward the viewpoint) alongside a reflected `bottle` to their left. Across frames 1–3, the child remains in the lower center looking up toward the camera wearer with their lower body cropped out of the bottom of the frame, while the segmented counter bottles shift slightly as the head-mounted camera moves; in frames 4–5, as the camera turns rightward toward the sink and toilet, no masks are detected at all. This map makes it easier than the RGB image to distinguish individual overlapping bottles on the cluttered left counter in frames 2–3 and highlights the reflected person and bottle in frame 1 against the monochromatic yellow background. However, it is highly unreliable: in frame 1 it misclassifies the toilet paper roll, caddy, and counter items on the right (~0.6–0.8 m away) as a large `banana`, merges the child and camera wearer into a single `person` mask in the mirror, misses the toothbrush and bathroom fixtures (sink, toilet, mirror) entirely, and fails to detect the child's head at the bottom of frame 4 or any objects in frames 4–5.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is completely blank in frames 1, 2, 4, and 5, and in frame 3 renders only a small yellow body-skeleton fragment in the lower-central foreground (~0.3–0.5 m from the camera wearer) corresponding to the child standing in front of the sink. In frame 3, this partial skeleton places keypoints near the child's head/face and upper torso/shoulder area within arm's reach directly below and in front of the camera wearer, where the RGB frame shows the child facing and looking upward toward the wearer while holding or standing beside an upright toothbrush. As the sequence progresses from frames 1–2 into frame 3 and then turns up and rightward toward the toilet in frames 4–5, the pose detector only briefly registers the child in frame 3 before losing them as they drop out of the lower-left field of view. While the single detection in frame 3 roughly confirms the location and slight tilt of the child's upper body despite the heavy privacy blur over the face in RGB, it provides almost no structural detail beyond what is visible in the colour image. The pose map is largely unreliable across the strip because heavy face blurring, steep downward egocentric viewing angles, and truncation at the bottom frame edge cause it to miss the child entirely in frames 1, 2, and 4, miss the camera wearer's and child's bodies reflected in the upper mirror (~0.8–1.0 m away), and fail to detect the visible hand holding the toothbrush at the bottom center of frames 1–3.
